guest.titre: Head of Applied Research and Analytics
guest.bio_context: Stephen Bushbaum is Head of Applied Research and Analytics at Trep, a data modeling and analytics firm for the CMBS, commercial real estate and CLO markets. He develops analytical frameworks to understand commercial real estate market dynamics, including the three-clock system (property, capital, and credit clocks) used to analyze how different market signals synchronize during maturity events.

context.real_quote: Maturity is the great synchronization event that forces all of these clocks to come into sync.

context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the Trep Wire podcast, the show where commercial real estate needs data and insights. This is a special edition of our Week in Review for the week ending September 11, 2026. I'm Haley Keene with Trep, a data modeling and analytics firm for the CMBS, commercial real estate and CLO markets. I'm with Lonnie Hendry, Chief Product Officer, and Stephen Bushbaum, Head of Applied Research and Analytics. This week, we're bringing you a special edition of the show, which we recorded live at the California MBA Western States CREF Conference in Las Vegas. We took the stage for a conversation called Beyond the Headlines, what the data really says about Western CRE. We looked at why some of the signals in commercial real estate seem to contradict each other right now, then dug into what the data is showing across Western office, life sciences, multifamily, and self-storage. We also got into the maturity wall ahead, why the story can change pretty dramatically from one market to the next, and two individual deals that show just how differently property performance, financing, and credit can play out. So for this week's episode, we're bringing you that full live conversation. Let's get into the show. The Trapwire team. Thank you so much, Cody, and thank you to the entire organization here at the California MBA for having us. We're so excited to do a live version of our show here. What we're doing right now is we're actually recording with these mics and we'll release it across our channels tonight. So we started our podcast, like Cody said, back in March 2020. It's a weekly show just to try to make sense of the news and how it's impacting commercial real estate. We didn't think we'd have so much to talk about every week, but six plus years later, we're still going. And that's why we kind of want to jump in right away here. We have a lot to cover. If you're a listener, you know we try to squeeze a lot into an almost hour-long episode, but we want to make it interesting. We want to share some data and tidbits and really give a behind-the-scenes look at commercial real estate. So we call today's session Beyond the Headlines because, as you all know, you're following the commercial real estate markets every day. The topics, the headlines, even the individual data points that you may see can sometimes contradict one another. Leasing can be improving while credit conditions are deteriorating. Capital can come back before fundamentals fully recover at the property. And sometimes a property with weakening fundamentals can refinance when a stronger one can't. So we've been trying to make sense of why all of this is occurring at once. And Stephen, you have a pretty useful framework for looking at this. Why don't you kick us off here and walk us through it? Love to. So when we read through the headlines, we get this mixture of positive and negative at the same time. And trying to come up with a framework to digest it is what brought us to this idea of a three-clock system. You have the property clock that deals with your leasing and occupancy, your property income statement. So basically, the property fundamentals. Then you have the capital clock that's dealing with capital market conditions. So what's your underlying coupon on the loan? What do, well, broader refinancing conditions look like in the market and your cost of capital? And then, well, your loan structure. When is your refinancing pressure going to come up? Then you have your credit clock. So are you just on the watch list? You're still current on payments. You're not yet delinquent, but there's clearly some concerns that have crept up. Or have you progressed to, say, payment default? Or, I mean, it goes this way. It's oftentimes a receiver gets put in place and it looks like it's headed toward foreclosure. Or maybe you're staving that off and you're working through toward a modification outcome. So we have these three clocks, the property, the capital, and the credit clock. And w

pending_qa.q: What median coupon rate applies to commercial real estate refinancings year-to-date in 2026?
pending_qa.r: The median coupon for commercial real estate refinancings year-to-date in 2026 is approximately 6.44%. This creates significant refinancing pressure for properties that locked in fixed-rate debt at lower rates in 2019 or 2020, where borrowers may have three or four percent mortgages that would refinance at substantially higher rates.

pending_qa.q: What vacancy rate exists in major life sciences markets?
pending_qa.r: Life sciences markets are experiencing approximately 30% vacancy in major markets, a dramatic shift from the post-COVID period when demand for lab space was insatiable. This sector has experienced what Bushbaum describes as a bubble that has popped, with stimulus dialed back and demand significantly reduced.

pending_qa.q: What are the credit metrics and lease roll characteristics of the Genesis Towers life sciences property?
pending_qa.r: Genesis Towers demonstrates strong credit metrics with a debt service coverage ratio of 3.11 times coverage and current LTV of 44.2%, but faces significant operational challenges. The property has 73% current occupancy with 21% of space rolling in the next 12 months and 9% rolling between 13-24 months, meaning approximately one-third of the building is set to roll in two years. The loan matures in 2030 with a fixed coupon of just over 2.6%.

pending_qa.q: How much outstanding mortgage debt has hard maturities in September 2026 in the securitized market?
pending_qa.r: There is approximately $2.74 billion worth of hard maturities in September 2026 in the securitized data tracked by Trep, representing loans that have exhausted all extension options available to them. Of this total, approximately 50% have debt yields less than 8% and over 50% is office property.

pending_qa.q: What percentage of office debt set to mature in the Western U.S. over the next two years consists of soft maturities?
pending_qa.r: Slightly over half of the total balance of office debt in the Western U.S. is set to mature over the next two years as soft maturities, meaning they have extension options remaining. However, most of these loans are far into their term with typically only one or two one-year extension options left, requiring a full refinancing cycle.
